prompt.context: You work at a large company which has many divisions. Each division uses different brands of computers and software packages. You are the new head of procurement at corporate headquarters.
prompt.question: How would you go about convincing the divisions to adopt a common standard if you do not have the power or authority to force the change? What advantages would there be if there were a unified standard?

clarifying_info.q: How many divisions are there and how many computers per division?
clarifying_info.a: Each division needs approximately 25 computers; assume there are many divisions totaling around 1,000 computers company-wide.

clarifying_info.q: Does each division currently run its own IT/help desk?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, each division apparently has its own help desk.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a target standard already identified?
clarifying_info.a: No, the task is to determine how to align on a standard and articulate the benefits.

framework: 1. Buying power / procurement savings: consolidating hardware and software purchases increases negotiating leverage with vendors (bulk pricing on computers, software licenses, peripherals).

2. Total cost of ownership (TCO): the purchase price is a small fraction of the true cost; ongoing costs include software, accessories, peripherals, tech support labor, and training — all reduced by standardization.

3. IT support consolidation: each division maintaining its own help desk is expensive and inefficient; a unified standard allows consolidation into a single help desk, reducing headcount via queuing-theory economies (each tech can serve any employee).

4. Persuasion / change management levers: since authority cannot be used, the case requires identifying incentives — cost sharing of savings, improved service levels, quicker support response, and reduction of stranded legacy costs.
5. Training efficiency: a single standard reduces training costs and shortens ramp time for new employees across all divisions.

questions.prompt: What are the primary financial benefits of a unified IT standard?
questions.guidance: Strong answer addresses two layers: (1) procurement savings from bulk purchasing — buying 1,000 computers vs. 25 at a time dramatically increases buyer power, yielding better pricing on hardware, software licenses, and accessories; (2) post-purchase TCO savings — tech support labor costs dwarf the hardware cost (e.g., a $5k laptop vs. the annual salary of a tech support employee), so consolidating help desks produces the larger savings. Candidate should mention queuing theory: a shared pool of technicians serving all employees needs fewer total headcount than N separate pools.

math.setup: Illustrative comparison: 40 divisions × 25 computers = 1,000 units. Buying individually at $1,000/unit vs. bulk price of, say, $700/unit.
math.answer: $300,000 hardware savings (illustrative); larger savings come from IT support consolidation.

questions.prompt: How would you convince the divisions to adopt the standard without having direct authority?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies carrots (not sticks): share the quantified cost savings with each division, offer improved SLAs (faster/better support), remove the burden of running their own help desk, and propose a governance model (cross-divisional steering committee) so divisions feel ownership. Candidate might also note identifying internal champions or pilot divisions to demonstrate ROI.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the cost categories and benefits associated with moving to a unified IT standard?

categories.name: Procurement / Hardware
ideas: Volume discounts on computers
Standardized peripherals (monitors, keyboards, printers) in bulk
Single vendor relationship / preferred pricing

categories.name: Software & Licensing
ideas: Enterprise-wide software licenses cheaper than per-division licenses
Single OS and application suite reduces compatibility issues
Easier to manage license compliance

categories.name: IT Support / Help Desk
ideas: Consolidate multiple divisional help desks into one
Queuing-theory efficiency: shared pool needs fewer agents
Each tech can support any employee, not just one division
Reduce duplicated tooling and internal applications

categories.name: Training
ideas: Single training curriculum for all employees
Shorter onboarding for new hires transferring between divisions
Reduced retraining when employees switch roles

categories.name: Security & Compliance
ideas: Uniform patch management and updates
Easier to enforce security policies
Single audit surface for compliance

categories.name: Change Management / Persuasion
ideas: Quantify and share savings projections with each division
Propose opt-in pilot with a willing division to prove value
Form a cross-divisional steering committee for buy-in
Offer transition support and migration assistance

recommendation: Recommend that corporate headquarters launch a voluntary standardization initiative, supported by a detailed TCO analysis showing each division the cost savings they would receive from consolidated purchasing and shared IT support.
Propose a cross-divisional steering committee to select the standard collaboratively, removing any perception of corporate imposition.
Pilot with one willing division, measure savings, and use results to attract remaining divisions organically.
risks: Divisions may resist if they have specialized software needs incompatible with the proposed standard.
Transition costs (migration, retraining) may be front-loaded, reducing near-term political support.
A 'golfing-buddy' dynamic (as noted in the case) may cause some division leaders to resist for non-economic reasons.
next_steps: Commission a TCO study with actual cost data from each division.
Identify two or three divisions as pilot candidates.
Establish the steering committee and agree on evaluation criteria for the standard.
Develop a migration roadmap and transition support package.
